===== src/assets.rs =====
//! Every static file this binary serves.
//!
//! Two directories, two rules. `assets/` is **fingerprinted** -- `site.css`
//! is published at `/css/site.<hash>.css`, so it can be cached forever and a
//! new build invalidates it by having a different name. `public/` is served
//! **verbatim**, because `robots.txt`, `favicon.ico` and anything linked to
//! from outside must keep the name they were given.
//!
//! Write a reference with `assets::url`, never by hand:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! <link rel="stylesheet" href={assets::url("css/site.css")}>
//! ```
//!
//! A name nothing publishes panics there rather than 404ing in a browser.
//!
//! Embedded, like the templates and the route table, so `serve` works from
//! any directory and nothing can go missing after the build passed. A file
//! added where there was none needs `touch src/assets.rs`, because nothing
//! referenced it yet.

brocanth_assets::assets!("assets", "public");
===== src/commands/api.rs =====
//! This application, from the outside.
//!
//! `cargo run -- api --help` lists every operation, because the list is
//! `crate::pages::described()` -- the same table the OpenAPI document is
//! built from, read off the handler signatures while this crate compiled.
//! There is nothing to regenerate: add a page and the client grows a
//! subcommand.
//!
//! ```text
//! $ cargo run -- api signup-post --handle ada-lovelace --age 36
//! {"id":"0191a3f0-0000-7000-8000-000000000000","handle":"ada-lovelace"}
//! ```
//!
//! The flags come from the request body's own schema, and their help text
//! is the sentence each field carries. Nothing here re-checks a rule: the
//! server is the authority, and a client that validated too would be a
//! second opinion that can disagree with it.

use brocanth_command::{anyhow, clap, cmd, Command, Context};

/// Call this application's own API.
#[cmd]
#[derive(clap::Args)]
pub struct Api {
    /// The operation and its flags. `api --help` lists them.
    #[arg(trailing_var_arg = true, allow_hyphen_values = true, num_args = 0..)]
    pub rest: Vec<String>,
}

impl Command for Api {
    fn run(self, _ctx: &mut Context) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let routes = crate::pages::described();
        let wire = brocanth_client::Reqwest::new().map_err(anyhow::Error::msg)?;

        let mut argv: Vec<std::ffi::OsString> = vec!["api".into()];
        argv.extend(self.rest.into_iter().map(std::ffi::OsString::from));

        let answered =
            brocanth_client::run("api", &routes, &wire, argv).map_err(anyhow::Error::msg)?;

        println!("{}", answered.body);
        // The status is the exit code, so `api ... && something` means what
        // it looks like in a shell. The body is still printed, because a
        // 422 from this framework carries every fault and that is the part
        // worth reading.
        if !answered.ok() {
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
===== src/commands/css.rs =====
//! `css` -- build assets/css/site.css from assets/css/_tailwind.css.
//!
//!     brocanth css          once, minified
//!     brocanth css -W       again on each change
//!
//! Ordinary project code, like `serve`: rename it, give it more flags, or
//! delete it. It is here rather than in a shell script because this project
//! already has a command line, and a second way to run things is a second
//! thing to keep in step.
//!
//! The Tailwind CLI comes out of `node_modules` and there is no fallback to
//! `npx`. A fallback downloads some other version and hides the one fact
//! worth knowing, which is that nobody ran `npm install`.

use std::path::Path;
use std::process::Command as Child;

use brocanth_command::{anyhow, clap, cmd, Command, Context};

/// Build the stylesheet from the Tailwind input.
#[cmd]
#[derive(clap::Args)]
pub struct Css {
    /// Rebuild on each change instead of once.
    #[arg(short = 'W', long)]
    pub watch: bool,
}

const INPUT: &str = "assets/css/_tailwind.css";
const OUTPUT: &str = "assets/css/site.css";
const CLI: &str = "node_modules/.bin/tailwindcss";

impl Command for Css {
    fn run(self, ctx: &mut Context) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        // The project root and not the working directory: `brocanth css`
        // runs from wherever you happen to be, and every path below is
        // written relative to the project.
        let root = ctx.root();
        let cli = root.join(CLI);
        if !cli.is_file() {
            anyhow::bail!(
                "the Tailwind CLI is absent at {}\n       run `npm install` in {} first",
                cli.display(),
                root.display()
            );
        }

        let mut child = Child::new(&cli);
        child
            .current_dir(root)
            .args(["--input", INPUT, "--output", OUTPUT]);
        if self.watch {
            child.arg("--watch");
        } else {
            child.arg("--minify");
        }

        let status = child.status()?;
        if !status.success() {
            // No message beyond this: the CLI has already written its own
            // on the stderr this process inherited.
            anyhow::bail!("the Tailwind CLI failed");
        }

        // `--watch` only ever returns when it was interrupted, and the
        // output it leaves behind is whatever the last change produced.
        // Checking it, or touching the module below, would both be about a
        // build that is over.
        if self.watch {
            return Ok(());
        }

        let written = root.join(OUTPUT);
        let bytes = std::fs::metadata(&written)?.len();
        if bytes == 0 {
            anyhow::bail!("the build wrote no CSS to {}", written.display());
        }

        touch(&root.join("src/assets.rs"))?;
        println!("built {OUTPUT} ({bytes} bytes)");
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// Make cargo notice a stylesheet it has already compiled in.
///
/// The CSS is embedded at compile time, so a new one is a new binary, and
/// nothing rebuilds until the module that embeds it looks newer than the
/// artefact. Rewriting its own bytes is the portable way to say so: there is
/// no `utimes` in `std`, and a dependency for one call is not worth it.
fn touch(path: &Path) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let same = std::fs::read(path)?;
    std::fs::write(path, same)?;
    Ok(())
}
===== src/commands/routes.rs =====
//! Every route this application answers.
//!
//! `brocanth routes` builds this project and runs this command, so the
//! listing is the binary's own answer rather than a second reading of the
//! directory. The rows are `crate::pages::handlers()`, read off `src/pages`
//! while the crate compiled: a route is a file, so there is nothing to
//! regenerate and nothing that can fall behind.
//!
//! ```text
//! $ brocanth routes
//! VERB    PATTERN        HANDLER                      TAKES   GIVES
//! GET     /              pages::index::handle         -       -
//! GET     /about         pages::about::handle         -       -
//! POST    /signup        pages::signup::handle_post   Signup  Created
//! ```
//!
//! `TAKES` and `GIVES` are the body a handler reads and the `Json<T>` it
//! returns, from `crate::pages::described()`. A page that writes
//! `-> Result<impl IntoResponse, Error>` says neither, and prints `-`: the
//! wrapper is the opt-in, and these columns report it rather than ask for
//! it.
//!
//! An argument keeps the rows that contain it, in any column, so
//! `routes signup` is the one page and `routes POST` is every route that
//! writes.
//!
//! These are the pages. A plugin that mounts its own routes through a
//! `RouteSource` would not be in the list, and nothing this project has
//! mounts one -- so today the two are the same table. Say so here if that
//! stops being true.

use brocanth_command::{anyhow, clap, cmd, Command, Context};

/// List the routes this application answers.
#[cmd]
#[derive(clap::Args)]
pub struct Routes {
    /// Keep only the rows containing this text
    pub filter: Option<String>,
}

impl Command for Routes {
    fn run(self, _ctx: &mut Context) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let (header, mut rows) = table();
        if let Some(filter) = &self.filter {
            rows.retain(|row| row.iter().any(|cell| cell.contains(filter)));
        }
        if rows.is_empty() {
            // An application with no page and a filter that matched nothing
            // both print nothing, and only one of the two is the reader's
            // own doing.
            match &self.filter {
                Some(filter) => println!("no route matches `{filter}`"),
                None => println!("this application answers no route"),
            }
            return Ok(());
        }

        let mut widths: Vec<usize> = header.iter().map(|title| title.chars().count()).collect();
        for row in &rows {
            for (column, cell) in row.iter().enumerate() {
                widths[column] = widths[column].max(cell.chars().count());
            }
        }

        print_row(&widths, header.iter().copied());
        for row in &rows {
            print_row(&widths, row.iter().map(String::as_str));
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// One line, every cell padded to its column but the last.
///
/// The last is left alone, because trailing spaces are invisible until
/// something pipes this into a diff.
fn print_row<'a>(widths: &[usize], cells: impl Iterator<Item = &'a str>) {
    let mut line = String::new();
    for (column, cell) in cells.enumerate() {
        if column > 0 {
            line.push_str("  ");
        }
        if column + 1 == widths.len() {
            line.push_str(cell);
        } else {
            line.push_str(&format!("{cell:<width$}", width = widths[column]));
        }
    }
    println!("{line}");
}

/// The header, and one row per route.
///
/// Five columns, because this project has `input`: `described()` read every
/// handler's signature while the crate compiled, so what a route takes and
/// gives is known here and worth a column.
fn table() -> (Vec<&'static str>, Vec<Vec<String>>) {
    let described = crate::pages::described();
    let rows = crate::pages::handlers()
        .iter()
        .map(|(verb, pattern, handler)| {
            let shape = described
                .iter()
                .find(|row| row.verb == *verb && row.path == *pattern);
            let takes = shape
                .and_then(|row| row.takes.as_ref())
                .and_then(|node| node.name())
                .unwrap_or("-");
            let gives = shape
                .and_then(|row| row.gives.as_ref())
                .and_then(|node| node.name())
                .unwrap_or("-");
            vec![
                verb.as_str().to_string(),
                (*pattern).to_string(),
                format!("pages::{handler}"),
                takes.to_string(),
                gives.to_string(),
            ]
        })
        .collect();
    (vec!["VERB", "PATTERN", "HANDLER", "TAKES", "GIVES"], rows)
}

// The parameters are this page's contract with its handler. Rename one and
// src/pages/about.rs stops compiling, which is the point.

pub fn About(title: &str, verb: &str, path: &str) -> Element {
    <h1>About</h1>
    <p>
        You asked for <code>{verb} {path}</code>. This page answers GET
        and nothing else, so a DELETE to it is a 405 carrying
        an <code>Allow</code> header rather than a 404.
    </p>
    <p>The shell around this is <code>src/pages/layout.rsx</code>, which {title} shares with every page.</p>

use crate::pages::views::link::Link;

// The page, and only the page. The document around it is layout.rsx, and
// this file does not know it exists.

pub fn Index(title: &str) -> Element {
    <h1>{title}</h1>
    <p>
        This file is <code>src/pages/index.rsx</code>, beside the handler
        in <code>index.rs</code>, and it is compiled into the binary. Edit it
        and cargo rebuilds; break it and the build stops on the line you broke.
    </p>
    <p>
        An interpolated value is escaped on the way out, always. Writing
        markup verbatim needs a different and greppable hole, so an injection
        is something you can search for rather than something you have to
        remember.
    </p>
    <ul>
        <li><Link to="/about">/about</Link></li>
        <li><Link to={&crate::pages::routes::users::id::path(7)}>User 7</Link></li>
    </ul>
}
===== src/pages/layout.rsx =====
// The document every page in this directory, and every directory below it,
// is rendered inside. A page never names it: which layout wraps a page is a
// property of where the page is, which is the rule the Crystal page_router
// uses for layout.cr.
//
// A layout is an ordinary component with a parameter of type `Element`, and
// `children` is the only parameter `html!` fills -- it cannot know what a
// second one would mean. A value every page shares comes from a const, as
// the title does here; a value belonging to one request belongs on the page
// component, which the handler builds and which already has the context.

use crate::pages::TITLE;

pub fn Layout(layout: &str, children: Element) -> Element {
    <!DOCTYPE html>
    <html lang="en">
        <head>
            <meta charset="utf-8">
            <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
            <title>{TITLE}</title>
            <link rel="stylesheet" href={crate::assets::url("css/site.css")}>
            <script src={crate::assets::url("dpswap.min.js")} defer></script>
        </head>
        <body class="min-h-screen bg-white text-slate-900">
            <header><a href="/">{TITLE}</a></header>
            <main dp-layout={layout} id="outlet">{children}</main>
        </body>
    </html>
}
===== src/pages/link.rsx =====
// An anchor that swaps instead of reloading the document.
//
// Written as a real <a href> and enhanced afterwards. With JavaScript off,
// to a crawler, and on the first load of any page it is a link and the
// browser does what it always did -- which is why `to` is required and why
// there is no version of this that renders a <span> with a click handler.
//
// `to` takes what the route helpers return:
//
//     <Link to={routes::users::id::path(7)}>User 7</Link>
//
// never a string. A route that does not exist is then a compile error
// rather than a 404 somebody finds later.

pub fn Link(to: &str, children: Element) -> Element {
    <a href={to} dp-boost>{children}</a>
}
===== src/pages/openapi.json.rs =====
//! `/openapi.json` -- because the file is called `openapi.json.rs`.
//!
//! The route is the file name, as it is for every page: the last dot is the
//! extension and what is left is the path, so this file answers
//! `/openapi.json` and renaming it moves the document.
//!
//! The body was rendered once, at startup, by `src/plugins/openapi/mod.rs`.
//! This page hands it out and does nothing else.

use crate::pages::{Ctx, Error, IntoResponse};

/// GET `/openapi.json`.
///
/// `no-cache` rather than a long max-age: the document changes when this
/// application is redeployed, and a client holding a stale one is the exact
/// failure a derived document exists to prevent.
pub fn handle(_ctx: &mut Ctx) -> Result<impl IntoResponse, Error> {
    let body = crate::plugins::openapi::json().ok_or_else(|| {
        Error::internal("the openapi plugin is not registered, so there is no document to serve")
    })?;
    Ok((
        body.to_string(),
        200,
        vec![
            ("content-type".to_string(), "application/json".to_string()),
            ("cache-control".to_string(), "no-cache".to_string()),
        ],
    ))
}

/// GET `/openapi.yaml`.
pub fn handle(_ctx: &mut Ctx) -> Result<impl IntoResponse, Error> {

    })?;

        body.to_string(),

===== src/pages/status.jt =====
// The body of `/status`. A template is a function whose body is JSON with
// holes, and the macro compiles it into straight-line writes: every static
// run below is one memcpy, and the commas are resolved while this file is
// compiled rather than counted when a request arrives.
//
// Take parameters by reference. A `&str` is borrowed into the template and
// nothing is copied to render it.

pub fn Status(name: &str, version: &str, parts: &[&str]) -> Json {
    "name": name,
    "version": version,
    "ok": true,
    "parts": [ for p in parts { p } ],
}
===== src/pages/status.rs =====
//! `/status` -- because the file is called `status.rs`.
//!
//! The answer is JSON, and its shape is in `status.jt` beside this file.
//! Nothing here builds a struct for the response: the template is the
//! shape, and it is compiled into the binary rather than parsed per
//! request.

use crate::pages::{payload, render_json, Ctx, Error, IntoResponse};

/// GET. The verb comes off the function name, the same as every other page.
pub fn handle(_ctx: &mut Ctx) -> Result<impl IntoResponse, Error> {
    render_json(payload::status::Status(
        env!("CARGO_PKG_NAME"),
        env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"),
        &["pages", "router"],
    ))
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn the_template_is_the_shape_of_the_answer() {
        // Rendered without a request, because a template takes values and
        // not a context. Edit `status.jt` and this is what changes.
        let body = jt::to_string(&payload::status::Status("api", "0.1.0", &["pages"]));
        assert_eq!(
            body,
            r#"{"name":"api","version":"0.1.0","ok":true,"parts":["pages"]}"#
        );
    }

    #[test]
    fn the_answer_says_it_is_json() {
        let answered = render_json(payload::status::Status("api", "0.1.0", &[])).expect("renders");
        assert!(answered
            .headers
            .iter()
            .any(|(name, value)| name == "content-type" && value == "application/json"));
    }
}

// Wraps every page under src/pages/users/, inside the root layout rather
// than instead of it. Nothing declares the stacking: `html!` reads it off

    </section>
}
===== src/plugins/admin/mod.rs =====
//! The backoffice, at `/admin`.
//!
//! Written once by `brocanth create`. This file is yours.
//!
//! It ships locked, and two answers are yours to give:
//!
//! 1. **Who may open a screen.** The policy is `DenyAll` until
//!    `AdminConfig::with_policy` names another, so every screen answers 403.
//! 2. **Who is asking.** [`principal`] returns an anonymous principal until
//!    it reads your user off the request.
//!
//! It has no models yet. A model needs a data source that reads its rows and
//! a row policy: `AdminConfig::resource(..)`, one per model. A model with no
//! resource answers 403 on every screen. `brocanth_admin::rows` has the
//! worked example, and `brocanth-admin-model` is the data source over
//! SeaORM.
//!
//! The routes are in the one table `src/pages/mod.rs` builds:
//! `pages::mounted` calls [`mount`] with the prefix. A page at `/admin` is
//! therefore a build error, not a race.

use std::future::Future;
use std::sync::Arc;

use brocanth::routing::{BuildError, RouterBuilder, Verb};
use brocanth_admin::policy::Principal;
use brocanth_admin::{Admin, AdminConfig, Fixture, Submission};

use crate::pages::{Ctx, Handler, Response};

/// Every screen of the admin, under `prefix`.
///
/// Four routes: the index and everything under it, for GET and for POST.
/// The admin parses its own paths, so the table gives it the whole path and
/// does not split it into twelve routes.
pub fn mount(routes: &mut RouterBuilder<Handler>, prefix: &str) -> Result<(), BuildError> {
    let admin = Arc::new(Admin::new(
        // An empty in-memory source: no models, so no rows to read. Put
        // your own `AdminData` here, or `brocanth_admin_model::admin_source!`
        // over your database connection.
        Arc::new(Fixture::new()),
        AdminConfig::new().titled("My Blog admin").at(prefix),
    ));
    let rest = format!("{}/{{*rest}}", prefix.trim_end_matches('/'));
    for pattern in [prefix, rest.as_str()] {
        routes.route(pattern, Verb::Get, screen(Arc::clone(&admin)))?;
        routes.route(pattern, Verb::Post, screen(Arc::clone(&admin)))?;
    }
    Ok(())
}

/// One handler for every screen. The admin reads the path and decides.
fn screen(admin: Arc<Admin>) -> Handler {
    Box::new(move |ctx: &mut Ctx| {
        let ctx = &*ctx;
        // HEAD reaches the GET handler, and the admin knows two verbs.
        let method = match ctx.verb {
            Verb::Post => "POST",
            _ => "GET",
        };
        let form = submission(ctx);
        let who = principal(ctx);
        // `?` on the admin's own failure: a data source that failed, or a
        // template that did not render. A refusal is not one: it is a page.
        let answer = wait(admin.dispatch(who, method, &ctx.path, &ctx.query, &form))?;
        Ok(match answer {
            brocanth_admin::Response::Page { status, html } => Response::new(status, html),
            brocanth_admin::Response::Redirect { status, location } => {
                Response::empty(status).with_header("location", location)
            }
        })
    })
}

/// Who is asking, as the admin's policy sees it.
///
/// Anonymous until this reads your user off the request. When a plugin
/// publishes one, this is one line:
///
/// ```ignore
/// ctx.provided::<CurrentUser, _>()
///     .map_or_else(Principal::anonymous, |user| Principal::new(user))
/// ```
fn principal(_ctx: &Ctx) -> Principal<'_> {
    Principal::anonymous()
}

/// The form a POST sent. Anything that is not urlencoded is an empty form,
/// so the screen shows its errors and writes nothing.
fn submission(ctx: &Ctx) -> Submission {
    let urlencoded = ctx
        .content_type()
        .is_some_and(|t| t.starts_with("application/x-www-form-urlencoded"));
    match ctx.body_text() {
        Some(body) if urlencoded => Submission::from_urlencoded(body),
        _ => Submission::new(),
    }
}

/// Runs the admin's answer to completion on this thread.
///
/// The admin is async because a database is, and a handler in this table is
/// not. Under `serve` the runtime has worker threads, so this tells tokio the
/// thread blocks. Anywhere else, such as a test, the admin's own small
/// executor runs it.
fn wait<F: Future>(future: F) -> F::Output {
    use tokio::runtime::{Handle, RuntimeFlavor};
    match Handle::try_current() {
        Ok(handle) if handle.runtime_flavor() == RuntimeFlavor::MultiThread => {
            tokio::task::block_in_place(|| handle.block_on(future))
        }
        _ => brocanth_admin::rt::block_on(future),
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use brocanth::routing::{Dispatch, Verb};

    use crate::pages::Ctx;

    /// The admin is in the table, and it answers 403 until somebody opens it.
    #[test]
    fn the_admin_is_mounted_and_ships_locked() {
        let router = crate::pages::router().expect("the table builds");
        let Dispatch::Found { handler, matched } = router.dispatch(Verb::Get, "/admin") else {
            panic!("/admin is not in the table");
        };
        let mut ctx = Ctx::new(Verb::Get, "/admin", matched.params());
        let answer = handler(&mut ctx).expect("the admin answers");
        assert_eq!(answer.status, 403);
    }
}
===== src/plugins/auth/mod.rs =====
//! Accounts and sessions, as this application registers them.
//!
//! One interface, no providers yet, and a local account path that does not
//! leak who has one: `register`, `login`, `request_password_reset` and
//! `verify_email` answer the same shape and take the same time whether or not
//! the address exists, because the expensive hash runs on both paths.
//!
//! `brocanth-auth` is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here, and through
//! no other route. Delete the registration in `src/app.rs` and delete this
//! file, and the application has no accounts and links nothing to hash a
//! password with.
//!
//! # Signing somebody in
//!
//! Everything is behind one context item, and a handler in an application
//! that never registered this plugin does not compile:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! use brocanth_auth::mfa::{Admission, Enrolled, FactorPolicy, FactorSet};
//!
//! let auth = ctx.provided::<Services, _>().expect("a dispatched request");
//!
//! // 1. The credential. `login` answers the same shape and takes the same
//! //    time whether or not the address has an account.
//! let who = auth.accounts().login(email, password).await?;
//!
//! // 2. What this account could prove. Nothing: `Mfa` needs a store trait
//! //    this application does not implement, so the enrolment is empty and
//! //    the constructor is named so that a reviewer stops on it. The day
//! //    there is an `MfaStore`, `Mfa::second_factors` answers this properly
//! //    and this line goes.
//! let enrolled =
//!     Enrolled::without_asking_the_store(who.account().id.clone(), FactorSet::empty());
//!
//! // 3. The policy, which consumes the proof. `Admitted` has no public
//! //    constructor, so this step cannot be skipped -- a sign-in that
//! //    forgot the second factor is a program that does not compile rather
//! //    than one that ships.
//! let Admission::Admit(admitted) =
//!     FactorPolicy::default().admit(&enrolled, who.into_proof())
//! else {
//!     return Err(Error::new(401, "sign in"));
//! };
//!
//! // 4. The session, which takes the admission by value.
//! let started = auth.sessions().begin_with_factors(admitted, None).await?;
//! // `started.cookie` is the `Set-Cookie` header to send back.
//! ```
//!
//! **A page cannot do that yet.** A handler here is
//! `Box<dyn Fn(&mut Ctx) -> Result<Response, Error>>`, which is synchronous,
//! and every method above is `async fn`. What runs today is a test, a
//! `manage` subcommand, and anything else of yours that already has a
//! runtime. The sign-in form arrives with the core's request hooks, which are
//! also what the two middleware offers below are waiting for.
//!
//! # Three decisions this file makes, each in one line
//!
//! They are type aliases so that changing one changes one line and nothing
//! else in the project changes type.
//!
//! 1. **`Store = MemoryStore`.** It is a `Mutex<HashMap>`. Accounts and
//!    sessions last exactly as long as the process, so a restart is a logout
//!    for everybody and a deploy loses every account. That is the one thing
//!    in this file to replace before anybody else uses this application: write
//!    an `AuthStore` over your database -- fourteen methods, of which the two
//!    that carry a requirement are a unique email and a `consume_token` that
//!    deletes and returns under one lock -- and change the line below.
//!
//!    When you do, the build moves: a pool is opened asynchronously and
//!    `Plugin::new` is not, so `configure` becomes `before_start` and reaches
//!    for the current runtime handle. `brocanth-cache` does it in about ten
//!    lines and they are worth copying rather than inventing.
//! 2. **`Http = StubHttp`.** There are no providers, so nothing in this
//!    binary ever performs a provider request, and a client that answers "no
//!    stubbed route" is a louder failure than one that opens a socket. It is
//!    also the line that keeps reqwest, rustls and their trees out of the lock
//!    file. Adding a provider changes it; see below.
//! 3. **`Passwords::recommended()`, not a setting.** The hash is argon2id and
//!    there is no choice to make. The one question a deployment gets to answer
//!    is cost, and it is a named constructor rather than three numbers in a
//!    file, because three numbers in a file is how an application ends up
//!    hashing at a cost nobody chose.
//!
//! # Adding a provider
//!
//! Three steps, and the flow code never learns the provider's name.
//!
//! 1. In `Cargo.toml`, `brocanth-auth = { ..., features = ["reqwest-client"] }`.
//! 2. Here, `pub type Http = brocanth_auth::http_client::ReqwestClient;`.
//! 3. Here, in `configure`, push one `ConfiguredProvider`:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! use brocanth_auth::oauth::ClientConfig;
//! use brocanth_auth::plugin::ConfiguredProvider;
//! use brocanth_auth::providers::catalog::GOOGLE;
//!
//! providers: vec![ConfiguredProvider {
//!     provider: GOOGLE,
//!     client: ClientConfig::new(
//!         std::env::var("GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID")?,
//!         std::env::var("GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET")?,
//!         "https://example.test/auth/google/callback",
//!     ),
//! }]
//! ```
//!
//! A provider is data -- endpoints, scopes, and a mapping from its profile
//! JSON to a common identity -- so the second one is another entry in that
//! `vec!` and no new code anywhere. `brocanth_auth::providers::catalog` has
//! the ones that are already written down.
//!
//! Two things change with the first provider. `same_site` below must become
//! `Lax`, because the callback is a cross-site top-level navigation and
//! `Strict` drops the cookie on the way back. And a matching email still does
//! not link an account to a provider: `Linking` returns a refusal the
//! application answers with a page that asks, because "this provider says
//! alice@example.com" is not Alice consenting, and several real products have
//! shipped that account takeover.
//!
//! # What is not here
//!
//! Second factors, one-time codes and login alerts. Each needs a store trait
//! of its own -- `MfaStore`, `OtpStore`, `SignInLocationStore` -- and
//! `brocanth-auth` deliberately keeps all three off `Auth`, so that an
//! application wanting a password form does not have to implement a TOTP
//! table. An application that wants them builds them here, from the same
//! `Arc<Store>`, and puts them on the context itself: one line each, in this
//! file, where the decision is visible.

use std::sync::Arc;

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::{ContextBuilder, ProvidesContext};
use brocanth_auth::http_client::StubHttp;
use brocanth_auth::plugin::AuthConfig;
use brocanth_auth::session::{SameSite, SessionConfig, SigningKey};
use brocanth_auth::{MemoryStore, Passwords, SystemClock};

/// Where identities, sessions and single-use tokens live.
///
/// In memory, for now. See the file header: this is the line to change first.
pub type Store = MemoryStore;

/// How this application reaches a provider.
///
/// It does not. There are no providers, so nothing calls this.
pub type Http = StubHttp;

/// Where the time comes from.
pub type Clock = SystemClock;

/// Everything a handler needs, behind one `Arc`: registration, login, the
/// token service, sessions and identity linking.
///
/// An alias rather than a wrapper, because `brocanth_auth::Auth` is already a
/// `ContextItem`. Cloning is cheap and the clone shares the provider key
/// cache, which is why there is one of these and not one per request.
pub type Services = brocanth_auth::Auth<Store, Http, Clock>;

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// Five values a file can carry. The store, the client, the clock and the
/// hasher are built below, because none of them is a thing a TOML file can
/// say.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[auth]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// The *name* of the environment variable holding the session signing
    /// key, not the key. 32 bytes, base64url.
    pub signing_key_env: String,
    /// The session cookie's name. `__Host-` in production: it is the only
    /// prefix a browser enforces, and what it enforces is `Secure`, a path of
    /// `/` and no `Domain` -- so a subdomain takeover cannot set a session
    /// cookie for the parent.
    pub cookie_name: String,
    /// Whether the cookie is `Secure`. False only on plain-HTTP localhost,
    /// and then the name above must lose its `__Host-` prefix as well.
    pub secure: bool,
    /// Seconds of inactivity before the session is dead.
    pub idle_timeout: i64,
    /// Seconds from creation before it is dead however much it was used.
    pub absolute_timeout: i64,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            signing_key_env: "MY_BLOG_SESSION_KEY".to_string(),
            cookie_name: "__Host-session".to_string(),
            secure: true,
            idle_timeout: 8 * 60 * 60,
            absolute_timeout: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60,
        }
    }
}

pub struct Auth {
    settings: Settings,
    /// Built at `configure`, so this is an `Option` for exactly the length of
    /// the build.
    services: Option<Services>,
}

impl Plugin for Auth {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = ProvidesContext<Services>;
    const NAME: &'static str = "auth";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            settings: config,
            services: None,
        }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if self.settings.cookie_name.is_empty() {
            return Err(PluginError::new("[auth] cookie_name must not be empty"));
        }
        // A `__Host-` cookie is `Secure` by definition, so a configuration
        // where the two disagree produces a cookie no browser stores and a
        // login that silently never takes. Caught here, at startup, where it
        // can still be answered.
        if self.settings.cookie_name.starts_with("__Host-") && !self.settings.secure {
            return Err(PluginError::new(
                "[auth] a __Host- cookie is Secure by definition; set secure = true, \
                 or drop the prefix for plain-HTTP development",
            ));
        }

        let name = self.settings.signing_key_env.clone();
        let raw = std::env::var(&name).map_err(|_| {
            PluginError::new(format!(
                "[auth] ${name} is not set. It is 32 random bytes, base64url:\n  \
                 export {name}=$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')\n\
                 There is no default: a key invented at startup would log every session \
                 out on each restart and differ between the instances of a fleet."
            ))
        })?;
        // Rejected rather than stretched. Padding a four-character secret to
        // 32 bytes is how a deployment ends up with a forgeable cookie and no
        // warning anywhere.
        let signing_key = SigningKey::parse(&raw)
            .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[auth] ${name}: {e}")))?;

        let passwords = Passwords::recommended()
            .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[auth] argon2id: {e}")))?;

        let session = SessionConfig {
            cookie_name: self.settings.cookie_name.clone(),
            secure: self.settings.secure,
            idle_timeout: self.settings.idle_timeout,
            absolute_timeout: self.settings.absolute_timeout,
            // Strict, and not the crate's own `Lax` default. `Lax` is there
            // for the cross-site top-level navigation an OAuth callback is,
            // and this application has no provider. Add one and this line
            // has to become `Lax` or the cookie is dropped on the way back.
            same_site: SameSite::Strict,
            // Path `/`, and thirty minutes for an impersonated session. Both
            // are the crate's defaults and both are arguments rather than
            // numbers; `SessionConfig` carries them.
            ..SessionConfig::default()
        };

        // Nothing here opens anything, so there is no `before_start`:
        // `MemoryStore` is a `HashMap` and `Auth::build` is synchronous. A
        // store over a database is a pool, a pool is opened asynchronously,
        // and `Plugin::new` is not async -- so that swap moves this block
        // into `before_start`, where it takes the current runtime handle and
        // blocks on a scoped thread. `brocanth-cache` does exactly that.
        self.services = Some(
            brocanth_auth::Auth::build(AuthConfig {
                store: Arc::new(Store::new()),
                http: Arc::new(Http::new()),
                clock: Arc::new(SystemClock),
                signing_key,
                session,
                passwords: Arc::new(passwords),
                // Add one here. The file header has the three lines.
                providers: Vec::new(),
            })
            .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[auth] {e}")))?,
        );
        Ok(())
    }

    fn provide(&self, cx: &mut ContextBuilder) {
        // `configure` runs before the server is handed the application, so
        // the services are here by the time any request builds a context.
        if let Some(services) = &self.services {
            cx.insert(services.clone());
        }
    }
}
===== src/plugins/cache/mod.rs =====
//! The cache, as this application registers it.
//!
//! The cache is a table, and the table is `UNLOGGED`: Postgres writes no
//! write-ahead log for it, ships it to no replica, and truncates it on crash
//! recovery. For any other table that is a catastrophe. For a cache it is the
//! only state you can reason about, and it is what makes a cache in a
//! relational database defensible at all. A deployment that already runs
//! Postgres therefore gets a cache without running Redis.
//!
//! `brocanth-cache` is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here, and through
//! no other route. Delete the registration in `src/app.rs` and delete this
//! file, and the application caches nothing and links nothing to do it with.
//!
//! The crate also ships `CachePlugin`, and this is not that. `CachePlugin` is
//! handed a cache that is already open, because a pool is made asynchronously
//! and `Plugin::new` is not async. An application whose cache is one URL wants
//! the shorter road, so this plugin takes the URL, opens the pool at startup,
//! and publishes the same `CacheHandle`. Hand-built caches -- a shared pool, a
//! second namespace policy, a different backend -- are what `CachePlugin` is
//! for, and swapping to it is a change in this file alone.

use std::sync::Arc;

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::{ContextBuilder, ProvidesContext};
use brocanth_cache::{CacheHandle, PgCache};

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[cache]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// The Postgres URL the cache lives in. Postgres and nothing else, on
    /// purpose: a cache for a SQLite deployment is a separate crate behind the
    /// same `Cache` trait.
    pub url: String,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            url: "postgres://localhost/development".to_string(),
        }
    }
}

pub struct Cache {
    url: String,
    /// Open at `before_start` and not before, so the field is an `Option` for
    /// exactly the length of the build.
    handle: Option<CacheHandle>,
}

impl Plugin for Cache {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = ProvidesContext<CacheHandle>;
    const NAME: &'static str = "cache";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            url: config.url,
            handle: None,
        }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if self.url.is_empty() {
            return Err(PluginError::new(
                "[cache] url is required; there is no default cache",
            ));
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn before_start(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        // The lifecycle hooks are synchronous and opening a pool is not. This
        // is the manoeuvre `CachePlugin` makes, for the same reason: a server
        // process has a runtime, `block_in_place` is wrong on a current-thread
        // one, so take the handle and block the builder on a scoped thread.
        // This is startup, where blocking is what everybody expects.
        let runtime = tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current().map_err(|e| {
            PluginError::new(format!(
                "[cache] needs a Tokio runtime at startup to open its pool ({e})"
            ))
        })?;
        let url = self.url.clone();
        let cache = std::thread::scope(|scope| {
            scope
                .spawn(|| runtime.block_on(async move { PgCache::connect(&url).await }))
                .join()
                .map_err(|_| PluginError::new("the cache connection thread panicked"))?
                .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[cache] connecting: {e}")))
        })?;
        // The table is not created here. `brocanth-cache` can create it, and
        // it is off there for the reason it is absent here: the generator
        // proposes and the developer commits. `PgCache::schema_sql` hands out
        // the statements for a migration you can read.
        self.handle = Some(CacheHandle::new(Arc::new(cache)));
        Ok(())
    }

    fn provide(&self, cx: &mut ContextBuilder) {
        // `before_start` runs before the server is handed the application, so
        // the handle is here by the time any request builds a context.
        if let Some(handle) = &self.handle {
            cx.insert(handle.clone());
        }
    }
}
===== src/plugins/jobs/mod.rs =====
//! Background jobs, as this application registers them.
//!
//! A job is a struct that serialises, plus one `perform`. Enqueuing takes the
//! struct itself, so a payload a job cannot accept is a struct-literal error
//! rather than a decode failure on a worker at three in the morning.
//!
//! `brocanth-jobs` is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here, and through
//! no other route. Delete the registration in `src/app.rs` and delete this
//! file, and the application runs no jobs and links nothing to run them with.
//!
//! # Enqueuing, and what does not work yet
//!
//! This plugin publishes the `Queue` on the per-request context, and a
//! handler reaches it through `Ctx`:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! let queue = ctx.provided::<Queue, _>().expect("a dispatched request");
//! queue.enqueue(Welcome { user_id: 7 }).await?;
//! ```
//!
//! `provided` compiles only because this plugin is registered. Drop it and
//! the line stops building and names `Queue`, which is the whole reason
//! the provider list lives in the application's type.
//!
//! Anything else holding the `Queue` can enqueue too -- `src/app.rs`, a
//! command under `src/commands/`:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! queue.enqueue(Welcome { user_id: 7 }).await?;
//! ```
//!
//! The note here used to say a handler could not reach it, because `Ctx`
//! carried no context. It does now.
//!
//! # Where job types go
//!
//! `Welcome` is here so that this file compiles into something that runs.
//! Move it, and whatever follows it, into `src/jobs/` once there is more
//! than one -- the only thing that must stay here is the `register` call.
//!
//! **Register every job type before anything enqueues it.** A worker claims
//! by queue and not by name, so it will take a job whose name it does not
//! know, and a name it cannot resolve is a terminal failure: the row goes
//! straight to the dead letter rather than waiting for a worker that knows
//! it. The payload is kept and `Queue::requeue_dead` replays it, so nothing
//! is lost -- but the job does not run when you expected it to. During a
//! rolling deploy that means the old workers, so ship the registration
//! before you ship the first enqueue.
//!
//! The crate also ships `JobsPlugin`, and this is not that. `JobsPlugin` is
//! handed a queue that is already open, which is what an application with a
//! shared pool or a worker-only process wants. This one takes a URL, because
//! a new project has a URL.

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::{ContextBuilder, ProvidesContext};
use brocanth_jobs::{Job, JobContext, JobRegistry, Queue, Worker, WorkerHandle};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A job
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// Says hello, slowly, somewhere that is not a request.
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Welcome {
    /// Who to welcome.
    pub user_id: i64,
}

impl Job for Welcome {
    const NAME: &'static str = "welcome";
    /// Which queue it waits on. The worker below claims from the queues the
    /// config names, so a job on a queue nobody claims waits for ever.
    const QUEUE: &'static str = "default";
    type Error = std::io::Error;

    async fn perform(&self, _cx: &JobContext) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
        println!("welcome, user {}", self.user_id);
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// Every job type this application can run.
///
/// The one list that has to be kept: a worker claims a row by name and needs
/// the type to decode it. Adding a job is a type above and a line here.
fn registry() -> JobRegistry {
    let mut registry = JobRegistry::new();
    registry.register::<Welcome>();
    registry
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The plugin
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[jobs]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// The database the queue lives in. Its own URL, not the models': a
    /// queue and an ORM can share one database and need not.
    pub url: String,
    /// Create the three tables at startup if they are absent.
    pub migrate: bool,
    /// Run a worker in this process, as well as enqueuing from it.
    pub worker: bool,
    /// Which queues that worker claims from.
    pub queues: Vec<String>,
    /// How many jobs it runs at once.
    pub concurrency: usize,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            url: "postgres://localhost/development".to_string(),
            migrate: true,
            worker: true,
            queues: vec!["default".to_string()],
            concurrency: 5,
        }
    }
}

pub struct Jobs {
    settings: Settings,
    /// Opened at `before_start` and not before, so this is an `Option` for
    /// exactly the length of the build.
    queue: Option<Queue>,
    /// Kept so the worker can be stopped. The core's shutdown hook lands
    /// with the server layer; until then, dropping the application stops
    /// the process and the worker with it.
    worker: Option<WorkerHandle>,
}

impl Plugin for Jobs {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = ProvidesContext<Queue>;
    const NAME: &'static str = "jobs";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            settings: config,
            queue: None,
            worker: None,
        }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if self.settings.url.is_empty() {
            return Err(PluginError::new(
                "[jobs] url is required; the queue is a table and needs a database",
            ));
        }
        if self.settings.worker && self.settings.queues.is_empty() {
            return Err(PluginError::new(
                "[jobs] worker is true and queues is empty, so the worker would claim \
                 nothing; name a queue or set worker = false",
            ));
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn before_start(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        // The lifecycle hooks are synchronous and opening a pool is not. A
        // server process has a runtime, `block_in_place` is wrong on a
        // current-thread one, so take the handle and block the builder on a
        // scoped thread. This is startup, where blocking is expected.
        let runtime = tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current().map_err(|e| {
            PluginError::new(format!(
                "[jobs] needs a Tokio runtime at startup to open its pool ({e})"
            ))
        })?;

        let url = self.settings.url.clone();
        let migrate = self.settings.migrate;
        let queue = std::thread::scope(|scope| {
            scope
                .spawn(|| {
                    runtime.block_on(async move {
                        let queue = Queue::connect(&url).await?;
                        if migrate {
                            queue.migrate().await?;
                        }
                        Ok::<_, brocanth_jobs::Error>(queue)
                    })
                })
                .join()
                .map_err(|_| PluginError::new("the jobs connection thread panicked"))?
                .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[jobs] connecting: {e}")))
        })?;

        if self.settings.worker {
            // `enter` so that `start` finds the runtime to spawn on. The
            // worker is woken by the enqueue itself on Postgres rather than
            // polling; see `brocanth_jobs::listen`.
            let _guard = runtime.enter();
            self.worker = Some(
                Worker::builder(&queue)
                    .registry(registry())
                    .queues(self.settings.queues.clone())
                    .concurrency(self.settings.concurrency)
                    .start()
                    .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[jobs] starting the worker: {e}")))?,
            );
        }

        self.queue = Some(queue);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn provide(&self, cx: &mut ContextBuilder) {
        // `before_start` runs before the server is handed the application,
        // so the queue is here by the time any request builds a context.
        if let Some(queue) = &self.queue {
            cx.insert(queue.clone());
        }
    }
}
===== src/plugins/logging/mod.rs =====
//! Request logging.
//!
//! The core assumes no log layer at all -- not `log`, not `tracing`, not a
//! trait with a no-op default. This file is the whole of logging in this
//! binary: delete the registration in `main` and nothing logs, delete this file
//! and nothing about logging is compiled.

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, MiddlewareCatalog, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::NoContext;
use brocanth::routing::Next;

use crate::pages::{Ctx, Response};

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[logging]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// `error`, `warn`, `info` or `debug`.
    pub level: String,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            level: "info".to_string(),
        }
    }
}

pub struct Logging {
    level: String,
}

impl Plugin for Logging {
    type Config = Settings;
    /// Nothing on the context: a logger writes, it does not hand values out.
    type Provides = NoContext;
    const NAME: &'static str = "logging";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            level: config.level,
        }
    }

    fn configure_router(&mut self, catalog: &mut MiddlewareCatalog<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        // Offered, not mounted. Where it runs is the application's call, made
        // in `main`, at a pattern this file never sees.
        catalog.offer("request_log", "one line per request: verb, path, status");
        Ok(())
    }

    fn before_start(&mut self, lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        eprintln!("[{}] level {}", lc.instance(), self.level);
        Ok(())
    }
}

/// The layer `request_log` mounts.
///
/// A plain function is a layer: `Layer` is implemented for anything callable
/// with a context and the rest of the chain. Not calling `next.run` is how a
/// layer short-circuits, and dropping it is all that takes.
pub fn layer(ctx: &mut Ctx, next: Next<'_, Ctx, Response>) -> Response {
    let verb = ctx.verb;
    let path = ctx.path.clone();
    let response = next.run(ctx);
    eprintln!("{verb} {path} -> {}", response.status);
    response
}
===== src/plugins/model/mod.rs =====
//! The model layer.
//!
//! The ORM is recommended and absent. SeaORM is the recommendation, it is not a
//! dependency of the core and never will be, and it arrives through
//! `brocanth-model` -- which is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here and
//! through no other route. An application that stores nothing pays nothing for
//! it: not a crate in the lock file, not a section in the config, not a byte.
//!
//! The entity modules go under `src/models/`, and you write them by hand: a
//! struct deriving `DeriveEntityModel` with `#[brocanth_model::validates(..)]`
//! above it, as `brocanth_model`'s own documentation sets out. There is no
//! `brocanth generate model` -- the CLI scaffolds a project and adds a module
//! to one, and a generator for a single entity is not written yet.

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::{ContextBuilder, ContextItem, ProvidesContext};
use brocanth_model::ModelRegistry;

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[model]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// `sqlite://db/development.sqlite?mode=rwc`, or a Postgres URL.
    pub url: String,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            url: "sqlite://db/development.sqlite?mode=rwc".to_string(),
        }
    }
}

/// The handle a handler asks the context for.
pub struct Db {
    pub url: String,
}

impl ContextItem for Db {}

pub struct Model {
    url: String,
}

impl Plugin for Model {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = ProvidesContext<Db>;
    const NAME: &'static str = "model";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self { url: config.url }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        if self.url.is_empty() {
            return Err(PluginError::new(
                "[model] url is required; there is no default database",
            ));
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    fn before_start(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        // The pool opens here, at the last hook before the server is handed the
        // application, and drains on the matching shutdown hook.
        //
        // The registry below is what would make a generator and an admin UI
        // tractable: every entity compiled into this binary can be enumerated,
        // with its columns, nullability and keys. It reads an inventory that
        // `DeriveEntityModel` fills, so it counts every model linked in,
        // whoever wrote it. The count is zero until the first entity module
        // exists under `src/models/`, and the line is here so that it is not
        // a surprise when it fills.
        let registry = ModelRegistry::new();
        eprintln!("[model] {} entities registered", registry.names().len());
        Ok(())
    }

    fn provide(&self, cx: &mut ContextBuilder) {
        cx.insert(Db {
            url: self.url.clone(),
        });
    }
}
===== src/plugins/openapi/mod.rs =====
//! The OpenAPI document, as this application derives it.
//!
//! The route table already knows every path, every verb and every path
//! parameter, and it knows them while this crate compiles, because the
//! filesystem is the route table. So the document is derived from
//! `crate::pages::router()` rather than written, and the two cannot drift:
//! add a file under `src/pages` and the document grows an operation.
//!
//! `brocanth-openapi` is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here, and
//! through no other route. Delete the registration in `src/app.rs`, this file
//! and `src/pages/openapi.json.rs`, and the application describes nothing and
//! links nothing to describe it with.
//!
//! # What is derived, and what is not
//!
//! Every route, with its path parameters, an `operationId` and a 200. What a page takes and gives comes
//! from `pages::described()`, which `pages!` wrote off the handler
//! signatures: a second parameter is the request body, a `Json<T>`
//! return is the answer. Neither is written here, so neither can be
//! out of date.
//!
//! Anything else -- a summary, a second status, an example -- is added by
//! hand with `SpecBuilder::describe`, beside the lines below:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! .describe("/users/{id}", Verb::Get, |op| {
//!     op.summary("One user")
//! })
//! ```
//!
//! `/openapi.json` is hidden from the document it serves. The endpoint is a
//! row of the table it describes, and an endpoint that describes itself is
//! noise in every client somebody generates from this.
//!
//! # Why this is not `OpenApiPlugin`
//!
//! The crate also ships `OpenApiPlugin`, and this is not that. That one is
//! handed a document that is already built, which is right for an application
//! that writes its document in `main`. This one takes a title and a version,
//! because a new project has a title and a version. It still holds an
//! `OpenApiPlugin` and calls its hooks, so the two things only that type can
//! do still happen: an invalid document stops the build, and the document
//! reaches `Services` for anything else that wants to read it.

use std::sync::OnceLock;

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::NoContext;
use brocanth::routing::Verb;
use brocanth_openapi::{Format, OpenApiConfig, OpenApiPlugin, Schema, SpecBuilder};

/// Where the document is served.
///
/// A constant and not a setting. The path is the name of the file in
/// `src/pages` that answers it, so moving the document is renaming that file
/// and this line, and a setting that disagreed with the file name would serve
/// a 404 and hide it in the document.
pub const ROUTE: &str = "/openapi.json";

/// The rendered document, both ways round.
///
/// Rendered once at `configure`, so a request costs a borrow rather than a
/// walk of the whole structure. A `OnceLock` because the page that serves it
/// is a plain function with no handle on this plugin.
static RENDERED: OnceLock<(String, String)> = OnceLock::new();

/// The document as JSON, or `None` when this plugin was never registered.
pub fn json() -> Option<&'static str> {
    RENDERED.get().map(|(json, _)| json.as_str())
}

/// The document as YAML, or `None` when this plugin was never registered.
///
/// Served by `src/pages/openapi.yaml.rs`, which is the file beside the
/// JSON one and reads this instead.
pub fn yaml() -> Option<&'static str> {
    RENDERED.get().map(|(_, yaml)| yaml.as_str())
}

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[openapi]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// The name of the API, which is not the name of this binary.
    pub title: String,
    /// The version of the contract, not of the crate.
    pub version: String,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            title: "My Blog".to_string(),
            version: "0.1.0".to_string(),
        }
    }
}

pub struct OpenApi {
    settings: Settings,
    /// Built at `configure` and not in `new`, because deriving a document can
    /// fail and `Plugin::new` cannot.
    served: Option<OpenApiPlugin>,
}

impl Plugin for OpenApi {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = NoContext;
    const NAME: &'static str = "openapi";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            settings: config,
            served: None,
        }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        // The same function `src/app.rs` builds the live table with, so the
        // document describes what this binary actually dispatches.
        let router = crate::pages::router().map_err(|e| {
            PluginError::new(format!("[openapi] the route table does not build: {e}"))
        })?;
        let mut spec = SpecBuilder::new(self.settings.title.clone(), self.settings.version.clone())
            .routes_from_router(&router)
            .hide(ROUTE, Verb::Get);

        // What each page takes and gives. `pages!` read it off the handler
        // signatures, so the document says what the code does rather than
        // what somebody remembered to write down.
        for route in crate::pages::described() {
            if let Some(node) = &route.takes {
                spec = spec.describing_node(node);
            }
            if let Some(node) = &route.gives {
                spec = spec.describing_node(node);
            }
            let takes = route.takes.as_ref().and_then(|node| node.name());
            let gives = route.gives.as_ref().and_then(|node| node.name());
            spec = spec.describe(route.path, route.verb, move |mut op| {
                if let Some(name) = takes {
                    op = op.json_body(Schema::reference(name));
                }
                if let Some(name) = gives {
                    // A description is required and may not be empty, which
                    // the document's own validator says before anything is
                    // served. One sentence, the same for every operation,
                    // and `.describe(..)` is where a better one goes.
                    op = op.json_response(200, "The answer", Schema::reference(name));
                }
                op
            });
        }

        let document = spec
            .build()
            .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[openapi] deriving the document: {e}")))?;

        // The crate's own plugin, held rather than registered. Its
        // `configure` is what makes an invalid document a build failure
        // instead of a 500 found during an incident, and it renders both
        // bodies once.
        let mut served = OpenApiPlugin::new(OpenApiConfig::new(document).json_route(ROUTE));
        served.configure(lc)?;
        let _ = RENDERED.set((
            served.body(Format::Json).to_string(),
            served.body(Format::Yaml).to_string(),
        ));
        self.served = Some(served);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn register(&mut self, lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        // Publishes the document through `Services`, so a command or another
        // plugin can read it with `brocanth_openapi::document_of`.
        match &mut self.served {
            Some(served) => served.register(lc),
            None => Ok(()),
        }
    }
}
===== src/plugins/policy/mod.rs =====
//! Authorisation, as this application writes it.
//!
//! A rule is a predicate and a check is a witness. `PostPolicy` below is the
//! first; `Verified` is the second; the two are not alternatives.
//!
//! `brocanth-policy` is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here, and through
//! no other route. Delete the registration in `src/app.rs` and delete this
//! file, and the application has no rule algebra and links nothing to have one
//! with.
//!
//! # The bug this file cannot have
//!
//! PocketBase validates a rule against an empty request object, so a
//! misspelled field in a negated rule becomes `'' IS NOT 'banned'`, which is
//! true, which grants access -- silently, for ever. Two things here make that
//! impossible, and both are visible below:
//!
//! 1. **A field name is not a string.** `Pred::eq` takes a `PostColumn`, so
//!    `PostColumn::Autor` is a compile error. There is no
//!    `Pred::eq("author_id", ..)` to fall back to and no string-to-filter
//!    parser anywhere in this framework.
//! 2. **An absent value is a word somebody wrote.** An `Option` does not turn
//!    into a `Bound`. The author writes `Bound::or_deny`, `or_allow` or
//!    `or_null`, and the word is in the diff for a reviewer to disagree with.
//!
//! # Where the rules go
//!
//! `Post` is here so that this file compiles into something that runs. Move
//! it, and whatever follows it, into `src/policies/` once there is more than
//! one -- what must stay here is the plugin, because that is what reads the
//! dialect and puts it on the context.
//!
//! The column enum is written by hand on purpose: the `policy!` macro is
//! deliberately late, after a real application has used the algebra, so that
//! the syntax is informed rather than imitated.
//!
//! # Listing, and then writing
//!
//! A list is a `WHERE` fragment, so the paginator keeps its totals:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! let rules = ctx.provided::<Rules, _>().expect("a dispatched request");
//! let condition = PostPolicy.list(&visitor).condition::<Post>(rules.dialect)?;
//! // "SELECT .. FROM posts WHERE " + condition.sql(), bound to condition.binds()
//! ```
//!
//! A write is the same predicate carried into the statement, which is what
//! closes the window between the check and the change:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! let admission = PostPolicy.update(&visitor).admission::<Post>(rules.dialect, id)?;
//! let rows = /* run admission.query(), count the rows */;
//! let verified = admission.resolve(rows)?;          // zero rows is a denial
//! let write = verified.update(rules.dialect, [(PostColumn::Status, "published".into())])?;
//! // run write.query(); then:
//! write.applied(affected)?;                          // zero affected is RaceLost
//! ```
//!
//! `Verified` is taken by value everywhere it is used, and a debug build fails
//! the test that checked one and then forgot to spend it.
//!
//! # This project also has the broker
//!
//! `Pred::audience` is the join, and it is why `brocanth-realtime`
//! depends on this crate. A predicate you can inspect inverts into an
//! audience -- `author_id = 7` becomes the key `(author_id, 7)` -- so the
//! broker files a subscriber under that key and one write is a map lookup
//! rather than one query per subscriber. A rule that is a string can only
//! be executed, which is why PocketBase runs the query.

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::{ContextBuilder, ContextItem, ProvidesContext};
use brocanth_policy::{Bound, Column, Dialect, Entity, EntityPred, FieldMask, Ident, Policy, Pred};

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// An entity
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// The columns of `posts`, as an enum, because a rule is written in them.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub enum PostColumn {
    /// Primary key.
    Id,
    /// Who wrote it.
    AuthorId,
    /// `draft` or `published`.
    Status,
}

impl Column for PostColumn {
    /// Required rather than derived: a changed-field name that is not one of
    /// these is rejected instead of quietly permitted.
    const ALL: &'static [Self] = &[Self::Id, Self::AuthorId, Self::Status];

    fn name(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Self::Id => "id",
            Self::AuthorId => "author_id",
            Self::Status => "status",
        }
    }
}

/// The table the rules below are about.
pub struct Post;

impl Entity for Post {
    type Column = PostColumn;
    /// Checked at compile time, because a table name is program text and the
    /// only honest moment to reject one is while the program is being built.
    const TABLE: Ident = Ident::must("posts");
    const PRIMARY_KEY: Self::Column = PostColumn::Id;
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// A subject, and the rules about it
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// Whoever is asking. `brocanth-policy` never looks inside it.
///
/// An anonymous visitor is this application's own `None`, turned into a
/// decision at the point a rule reads it.
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Default)]
pub struct Visitor {
    /// The signed-in account, when there is one.
    pub account_id: Option<i64>,
    /// Whether this one may see everything.
    pub admin: bool,
}

impl Visitor {
    /// Nobody. What a request with no session carries.
    pub fn anonymous() -> Self {
        Self::default()
    }
}

/// The rules for `posts`.
///
/// Only `list` is required, because list authorisation is the one that cannot
/// be done per object: a paginator that filters after reading lies about its
/// totals. Everything else defaults to deny, which is what makes shipping this
/// file as it stands safe rather than lucky.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Default)]
pub struct PostPolicy;

impl Policy for PostPolicy {
    type Entity = Post;
    type Subject = Visitor;

    fn list(&self, who: &Visitor) -> EntityPred<Post> {
        if who.admin {
            // `Pred::is_always` reports this, so a test can assert which
            // subjects see everything.
            return Pred::Always;
        }
        Pred::any([
            Pred::eq(PostColumn::Status, "published"),
            // `or_deny` is the word that says what an anonymous visitor's
            // missing id means: they own nothing.
            Pred::eq(PostColumn::AuthorId, Bound::or_deny(who.account_id)),
        ])
    }

    fn create(&self, who: &Visitor) -> EntityPred<Post> {
        Pred::eq(PostColumn::AuthorId, Bound::or_deny(who.account_id))
    }

    fn update(&self, who: &Visitor) -> EntityPred<Post> {
        if who.admin {
            return Pred::Always;
        }
        Pred::eq(PostColumn::AuthorId, Bound::or_deny(who.account_id))
    }

    fn writable(&self, who: &Visitor) -> FieldMask<PostColumn> {
        if who.admin {
            FieldMask::except([PostColumn::Id])
        } else {
            // The author edits the body, never the status. The mask is the
            // other half of the rule: `update` says which rows, this says
            // which columns.
            FieldMask::only([PostColumn::AuthorId])
        }
    }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The plugin
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[policy]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// `postgres` or `sqlite`. A string here and an enum below: a config file
    /// is text, and the translation is checked at startup where a typo can
    /// still be answered.
    pub dialect: String,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            dialect: "sqlite".to_string(),
        }
    }
}

/// What this plugin puts on the context.
///
/// The dialect, and only the dialect. Every compile entry point still takes
/// one as an argument -- the call site says which it meant -- and this is
/// where the call site gets it, so one database is named once.
///
/// The policies are not here. `PostPolicy` is a unit struct and a value, not
/// a service: a handler writes `PostPolicy.list(&who)` and has nothing to
/// look up. What a handler cannot work out on its own is which dialect this
/// deployment is, so that is what the context carries.
pub struct Rules {
    /// Which dialect this application's conditions are compiled for.
    pub dialect: Dialect,
}

impl ContextItem for Rules {}

pub struct Policies {
    settings: Settings,
    /// Read at `configure` and not in `new`, because turning a string into a
    /// dialect can fail and `Plugin::new` cannot.
    dialect: Option<Dialect>,
}

impl Plugin for Policies {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = ProvidesContext<Rules>;
    const NAME: &'static str = "policy";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            settings: config,
            dialect: None,
        }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        let dialect = match self.settings.dialect.as_str() {
            "postgres" => Dialect::Postgres,
            "sqlite" => Dialect::Sqlite,
            other => {
                return Err(PluginError::new(format!(
                    "[policy] dialect is {other:?}; write postgres or sqlite"
                )))
            }
        };

        // Compile one rule at startup. It costs a string and it answers the
        // only question this file can get wrong without anybody noticing: a
        // column whose name is not a bare identifier fails the query rather
        // than escaping into it, and finding that out here is better than
        // finding it out on the first list request.
        let condition = PostPolicy
            .list(&Visitor::anonymous())
            .condition::<Post>(dialect)
            .map_err(|e| PluginError::new(format!("[policy] posts: {e}")))?;
        eprintln!("[policy] posts, anonymous: {}", condition.sql());

        self.dialect = Some(dialect);
        Ok(())
    }

    fn provide(&self, cx: &mut ContextBuilder) {
        // `configure` runs before the server is handed the application, so
        // the dialect is here by the time any request builds a context.
        if let Some(dialect) = self.dialect {
            cx.insert(Rules { dialect });
        }
    }
}
===== src/plugins/realtime/mod.rs =====
//! The realtime broker, as this application registers it.
//!
//! A subscription is an index entry, not a query. `brocanth-policy` is a
//! value rather than a string, so "the owner" inverts into `(author_id, 7)`,
//! the broker files the subscriber under that key, and a write becomes a map
//! lookup. PocketBase runs one `SELECT` per subscriber instead, which is
//! about 180 ms on Postgres at six hundred of them.
//!
//! `brocanth-realtime` is in `Cargo.toml` because this file is here, and
//! through no other route. Delete the registration in `src/app.rs` and delete
//! this file, and the application broadcasts nothing and links nothing to do
//! it with.
//!
//! # Publishing
//!
//! A handler that just wrote a row has the row, so it hands it over and the
//! broker reads nothing:
//!
//! ```ignore
//! // Not from a handler yet: `Ctx` has no extractor. See below.
//! let realtime = ctx.provided::<Broadcast, _>().expect("a dispatched request");
//! let row = Row::new().with("author_id", author);
//! realtime
//!     .broker
//!     .publish_with_row(&RowChange::created("posts", id), &row);
//! ```
//!
//! `src/app.rs` extracts it once at startup and prints the client limit,
//! which is there to be deleted: it exists so a brand-new project reads the
//! value it was given rather than warning that nothing does.
//!
//! # Reading
//!
//! The broker stops one layer short of the socket, on purpose: this
//! application's `Response` is a complete `Vec<u8>`, and every response hook
//! is specified to see one. A streaming body would skip compression, the
//! partial-navigation headers and `ETag` without saying so, so server-sent
//! events are a change to the core's hook contract rather than a type change
//! here.
//!
//! Three things read a mailbox today, none of them needing that change:
//!
//! 1. **In process.** `Broker::connect`, one subscription, and a thread on
//!    `Mailbox::recv_blocking`. This is how a cache invalidator or an audit
//!    log is written, and it is the reason to have a broker before there is a
//!    transport at all.
//! 2. **Long polling.** Keep the `Client` in the session; each request calls
//!    `Mailbox::recv_timeout` for a few seconds, then `Mailbox::drain`, and
//!    returns the frames as one finished body. Every hook runs exactly as
//!    specified. It costs a request per interval and a little latency.
//! 3. **Nothing.** The index costs what it holds, and an application that
//!    publishes without subscribers pays for a map lookup that finds no one.

use std::sync::Arc;

use brocanth::plugin_api::{Lifecycle, Plugin, PluginError};
use brocanth::plugin_context::{ContextBuilder, ContextItem, ProvidesContext};
use brocanth_realtime::{Broker, Config, Overflow};

/// What this plugin is built from.
///
/// It derives `Deserialize` because this application reads it from
/// `[realtime]` in a TOML file. Drop the config plugin and the derive goes
/// with it: `Plugin::Config` carries no bounds the core imposes.
#[derive(Debug, serde::Deserialize)]
#[serde(default, deny_unknown_fields)]
pub struct Settings {
    /// How many connections the broker will hold. At the limit `connect`
    /// refuses rather than evicting, so a new socket cannot displace an
    /// established one.
    pub max_clients: usize,
    /// How many topics one client may hold, so a client cannot spend the
    /// server's memory by asking.
    pub max_subscriptions_per_client: usize,
    /// How many frames a mailbox holds before the overflow policy fires.
    pub queue: usize,
    /// `drop-oldest`, `drop-newest` or `disconnect`. A string here and an
    /// enum below: the config file is text, and the translation is checked
    /// at startup where a typo can still be answered.
    pub overflow: String,
}

impl Default for Settings {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            max_clients: 1000,
            max_subscriptions_per_client: 64,
            queue: 32,
            overflow: "drop-oldest".to_string(),
        }
    }
}

/// What this plugin puts on the context.
///
/// A wrapper and not `Arc<Broker>` itself, because `ContextItem` is
/// brocanth's trait and `Broker` is `brocanth-realtime`'s type. That crate
/// deliberately does not depend on the core -- nothing in it touches a
/// request, a response or a route -- so the impl that joins the two belongs
/// in the one crate that can see both, which is this one.
pub struct Broadcast {
    /// The broker. Shared, so a clone is a pointer and every request sees
    /// the same index.
    pub broker: Arc<Broker>,
}

impl ContextItem for Broadcast {}

pub struct Realtime {
    settings: Settings,
    /// Built at `configure` and not in `new`, because reading the overflow
    /// policy out of a string can fail and `Plugin::new` cannot.
    broker: Option<Arc<Broker>>,
}

impl Plugin for Realtime {
    type Config = Settings;
    type Provides = ProvidesContext<Broadcast>;
    const NAME: &'static str = "realtime";

    fn new(config: Settings) -> Self {
        Self {
            settings: config,
            broker: None,
        }
    }

    fn configure(&mut self, _lc: &mut Lifecycle<'_>) -> Result<(), PluginError> {
        let overflow = match self.settings.overflow.as_str() {
            "drop-oldest" => Overflow::DropOldest,
            "drop-newest" => Overflow::DropNewest,
            "disconnect" => Overflow::Disconnect,
            other => {
                return Err(PluginError::new(format!(
                    "[realtime] overflow is {other:?}; write drop-oldest, \
